podcast.title: Early Career Slogging (2009-2015)
podcast.body: For six years prior to their mainstream breakthrough with the *Blurryface* album in 2015, 21 Pilots experienced "really hard slogging" during which they were largely unknown to the general public. Despite building a dedicated indie fanbase, they continued to play smaller venues. "But before that, we're six years of really hard slogging when almost no one knew who they were."

srcs.source: The Ongoing History of New Music
srcs.episode: Catching Up With Twenty One Pilots

podcast.title: Early Fanbase in Ohio (2011-2012)
podcast.body: By the time the band signed with Fueled By Ramen, 21 Pilots had cultivated a substantial fanbase within Ohio, capable of drawing nearly 2,000 attendees to their shows. However, their appeal outside the state was minimal, evidenced by one July 2011 gig attended by only 12 people. "Anyway, by this time, 21 pilots had a decent fanbase in Ohio, sometimes attracting almost 2,000 people to a show. Outside the state, not so much."

srcs.source: The Ongoing History of New Music
srcs.episode: Catching Up With Twenty One Pilots

podcast.title: Early Member Departures (2011)
podcast.body: In the spring of 2011, drummer Chris Salah left the band to prioritize his job at a music store, followed a month later by bassist Nick Thomas, who departed to focus on his university studies. Nick Thomas later returned to assist with the band's merchandise but not as a performing musician. "First of all, Chris Salah felt that he needed to spend more time at work. He had a job at a music store, and that seemed like something he needed to concentrate on."

srcs.source: The Ongoing History of New Music
srcs.episode: Catching Up With Twenty One Pilots

podcast.title: Josh Dunn Joining (2011)
podcast.body: In July 2011, Josh Dunn, a drummer who had considered pursuing studio work in Nashville, joined Tyler Joseph. Dunn was introduced by Chris Salah and was convinced to join after hearing Tyler's music. "However, Chris, remember the guy at the music store, knew someone at work named Josh Dunn. Josh was a drummer who had thought about getting some studio work in Nashville."

srcs.source: The Ongoing History of New Music
srcs.episode: Catching Up With Twenty One Pilots

podcast.title: Band Hiatus (2017-2018)
podcast.body: After completing two world tours in support of *Blurryface*, the band entered a period of hiatus starting July 6, 2017, which lasted almost a year. This break allowed Tyler Joseph and Josh Dunn to concentrate on creating new music without any interruptions or distractions. "After a couple of world tours in support of blurry face, the band went dark, on July 6, 2017, so Tyler and Josh could focus on music without any interruption or distraction."

srcs.source: The Ongoing History of New Music
srcs.episode: Catching Up With Twenty One Pilots

podcast.title: Chlorine Single Pre-Release Clue (2018)
podcast.body: Just prior to the release of the "Chlorine" single, the character Clancy posted a file on dmaorg.info titled "17-35.4527." These numbers represent the atomic number and atomic weight of the element chlorine, serving as an elaborate pre-release hint. "He and I assume it's a he, posted a file just before the release of chlorine as a single, with the name 17-35.4527."

srcs.source: The Ongoing History of New Music
srcs.episode: Catching Up With Twenty One Pilots

podcast.title: Demaorg.info Re-emergence (April 2018)
podcast.body: In April 2018, the dmaorg.info website was rediscovered by fans who found its address concealed within a gift image on the *Vessel* album page of the band's online store. The site's initial landing page displayed a cryptic error message warning, "404 error. You are in violation. They mustn't know you were here." "At April 2018, somebody was poking around the 21 pilots online store and found a website address hidden in a gift image on the page for the vessel album."

srcs.source: The Ongoing History of New Music
srcs.episode: Catching Up With Twenty One Pilots

podcast.title: Hidden Message in Text Post (2018)
podcast.body: A text posted on dmaorg.info, which preceded the "Chlorine" single, was subtly altered over several days. Fans who meticulously studied these changes could decipher that the alterations spelled out the name "Ned," the new character introduced in the "Chlorine" music video. "If you were paying attention and you studied the changes, you'd have discovered that the changes spelled out the name Ned, the name of the new character in the chlorine video."

srcs.source: The Ongoing History of New Music
srcs.episode: Catching Up With Twenty One Pilots

podcast.title: 12-inch Dance Remixes in the 2010s
podcast.body: A 12-inch dance remix of a Twenty One Pilots song was presented as an example of how, by the 2010s, such remixes were more likely to be co-opted and popularized by EDM culture rather than serving an alt-rock dance club scene as they would have in previous decades. "It's a 12-inch dance remix of a 21-pilot song. Yeah, I did say 21-pilots."

srcs.source: The Ongoing History of New Music
srcs.episode: The History of the 2010s Part 5: Music and Tech

podcast.title: Alt Rock Resurgence in the 2010s
podcast.body: Formed in 2009, Twenty One Pilots was instrumental in the brief return of Alt Rock to the mainstream Top 40 charts in the 2010s. Within five to six years of their formation, they were achieving billions of streams and earning gold and platinum albums. In 2016, they made history by becoming only the third rock act ever, after Elvis and The Beatles, to have two singles simultaneously in the Billboard Top Five. "They were formed in 2009, and within the next five or six years, they were streaming in the billions and having gold and platinum albums. In 2016, they became just the third rock act in history to have two singles in the billboard top five at the same time, only Elvis and the Beatles had managed that."

srcs.source: The Ongoing History of New Music
srcs.episode: The 100 Greatest Rock Moments of the Millennium So Far - Part 7: (40-31)

podcast.title: Backmasking in Digital Era
podcast.body: Twenty One Pilots is listed among the artists who have utilized backward messages in their recordings, a technique that made a comeback with the widespread availability of digital sound editing software from the late 1990s and early 2000s. "Back, cake, cold play, M&M, Fransford Nand, Lincoln Park, Marilyn Manson, Moby Soundgarden Tool, 21 Pilots, and a ton more."

srcs.source: The Ongoing History of New Music
srcs.episode: The Rock Explainer 5

podcast.title: Band Name Origin ("All My Sons")
podcast.body: The band's name is derived from Arthur Miller's 1947 play, "All My Sons," which is based on a true story. The play tells of an Ohio man who knowingly approved defective aircraft engines for use in World War II, leading to the deaths of 21 pilots. "This play is called All My Sons from 1947. And it's based on a true story about a man also from Ohio who conspired with the army to approve faulty and defective aircraft engines for use in combat in World War II. And as a result of this bad equipment, 21 pilots died."

srcs.source: The Ongoing History of New Music
srcs.episode: Catching Up With Twenty One Pilots

podcast.title: Band Name Spelling Choice
podcast.body: Tyler Joseph intentionally omits the hyphen between "20" and "1" in the band's name, prioritizing its visual design and how it appears in text or can be adapted into a logo or other graphic element. "But for Tyler, it's all about design. All about how it looks in text and how it can be adapted into a logo or other graphic design."

srcs.source: The Ongoing History of New Music
srcs.episode: Catching Up With Twenty One Pilots

podcast.title: Blurryface Album Narrative Theories
podcast.body: Members of the Skeleton Clique have actively developed and shared numerous theories on Reddit, attempting to connect all 14 songs on the *Blurryface* album into a coherent narrative. "If you dip into Reddit, which can be dangerous, you'll find a number of theories that attempt to link all 14 songs together into some sort of narrative."

srcs.source: The Ongoing History of New Music
srcs.episode: Catching Up With Twenty One Pilots

podcast.title: Blurryface Character (Doubt, Insecurity, Anxiety)
podcast.body: The *Blurryface* album's central concept revolves around a character named Blurryface, who serves as an avatar for Tyler Joseph's personal struggles with doubt, insecurity, and anxiety. Tyler physically embodies this character during live performances and video shoots by sporting black paint on his hands and neck. "The first thing we need to understand about blurry face is that it's centered on themes of doubt, insecurity, anxiety and a dollop of religion."

srcs.source: The Ongoing History of New Music
srcs.episode: Catching Up With Twenty One Pilots

podcast.title: Blurryface Twitter Account
podcast.body: An official Blurryface Twitter account exists and has amassed over 150,000 followers, despite never having posted a single tweet. "There is a blurry face Twitter account with over 150,000 followers, even though there have been zero tweets."

srcs.source: The Ongoing History of New Music
srcs.episode: Catching Up With Twenty One Pilots

podcast.title: Clancy's Journal (dmaorg.info)
podcast.body: Following the rediscovery of dmaorg.info, a series of posts from "Clancy's journal" began to appear on the site. These extensive journal entries are filled with complex clues pertaining to the upcoming *Trench* album and its songs. Clancy is also a significant character within the *Trench* storyline. "That was followed by a series of posts at dmaorg.info from Clancy's journal. These go on forever, but they're filled with clues about the album and songs to come."

srcs.source: The Ongoing History of New Music
srcs.episode: Catching Up With Twenty One Pilots

podcast.title: Dema City and Mythology (Trench Album)
podcast.body: The *Trench* album introduces a deeply layered world centered around the city of Dema, a name that, in the religion of Zoroastrianism, translates to "tower of silence" (a place where dead bodies are exposed to vultures). This fictional world features nine "bishops," with Niko as the chief bishop. "It describes a world built around the city of dma, which translated from the religion of Zoroastrianism, means tower of silence."

srcs.source: The Ongoing History of New Music
srcs.episode: Catching Up With Twenty One Pilots

podcast.title: Discontinuation of Regional At Best
podcast.body: The album *Regional At Best* was discontinued and effectively wiped from existence as a contractual condition of 21 Pilots' signing with Fueled By Ramen in April 2012. While physical copies are now rare and can fetch prices ranging from $35 to $900 online, a double Tinderbox version is listed as being blocked from sale. "A condition of the deal was that 21 pilots had to make the Regional At Best album disappear."

srcs.source: The Ongoing History of New Music
srcs.episode: Catching Up With Twenty One Pilots

podcast.title: Elaborate Online Worlds
podcast.body: Twenty One Pilots (referred to as "21 pilots" in transcript) is noted for creating elaborate online worlds and stories, often starting with a clue embedded within an image connected to an album or song. This approach allows for fans to "go down a rabbit hole" and engage in a more elaborate and interactive experience. "And then we have 21 pilots. They've learned a great length to create elaborate worlds and stories online, and often begin with a clue found within an image connected to an album or a song."

srcs.source: The Ongoing History of New Music
srcs.episode: Digital Debris Part 2: Album Artwork

podcast.title: Grassroots Beginnings (Ohio)
podcast.body: In their formative years, 21 Pilots operated in a very independent, "do it yourself" manner, playing gigs wherever possible. Tyler Joseph's mother would promote their shows by distributing tickets outside Ohio State University games. The band also participated in battle of the bands events and performed alongside hardcore groups. "Tyler's mum would actually stand outside Ohio State University Games, giving away ticket to her kid show."

srcs.source: The Ongoing History of New Music
srcs.episode: Catching Up With Twenty One Pilots

podcast.title: Hidden Website Address (dmaorg.info)
podcast.body: An obscure website address, dmaorg.info, can be discovered by navigating to the *Vessel* album page on the 21 Pilots online store. This site serves as a central hub for the band's elaborate mythology, featuring messages and posts from a character named Clancy. "if you go to the 21 pilots online store and navigate to the page where their third album vessel, you might be able to find a hidden website address, which is dmaorg.info."

srcs.source: The Ongoing History of New Music
srcs.episode: Catching Up With Twenty One Pilots

podcast.title: High School Origins (Columbus, Ohio)
podcast.body: Frontman Tyler Joseph grew up in Columbus, Ohio, where his mother was a teacher and his father a high school principal and basketball coach. Tyler initially excelled at basketball, playing point guard, before turning his focus to music. "At the center of everything is Tyler Joseph of Columbus, Ohio. Mom was a teacher, dad was a high school principal and basketball coach."

srcs.source: The Ongoing History of New Music
srcs.episode: Catching Up With Twenty One Pilots

podcast.title: Intricate World Building
podcast.body: 21 Pilots is noted for creating an immersive and complex fantasy world for their fans, filled with deep mythology, intricate clues, and Easter eggs across their music and online platforms. This level of detail encourages fans to explore and become deeply involved in the band's invented universe. "If you're looking to lose yourself in this fantasy world created by the band, you will be gone for a very, very long time."

srcs.source: The Ongoing History of New Music
srcs.episode: Catching Up With Twenty One Pilots

podcast.title: Metadata Spelling of Band Name and Song Titles
podcast.body: Twenty One Pilots serves as an example for metadata challenges, specifically the directive not to hyphenate their band name ("Twenty-One Pilots"), and the compounding issue of song titles often being spelled as single words. "Now remember, you do not split their name with a hyphen. If you do put a hyphen between 20 and one, then that's a metadata issue."

srcs.source: The Ongoing History of New Music
srcs.episode: 23 Points About Streaming: Part 2

podcast.title: New Band Logo (Blurryface Era)
podcast.body: Coinciding with the *Blurryface* album, a new band logo emerged, composed of a bar, a hyphen, and a slash, all standard computer keyboard characters. Fans are encouraged to interpret and adapt this symbol into their own versions of the 21 Pilots logo. "A new band logo appeared around this time. It's a bar, a hyphen and a slash from a standard computer keyboard."

srcs.source: The Ongoing History of New Music
srcs.episode: Catching Up With Twenty One Pilots

podcast.title: Niko's Name Origin
podcast.body: The character Niko, one of the nine bishops of Dema, derives his name from Nicholas Bourbaki, a pseudonym used by a group of French mathematicians in the 1930s. Within the *Trench* mythology, Nicholas Bourbaki is revealed to be the true identity of Blurryface, the central character from the previous album. "The name Niko is derived from Nicholas Borbacchi, which was a pseudonym used by a bunch of real-life French mathematicians back in the 1930s, who did some really esoteric things with numbers that I can't even begin to understand."

srcs.source: The Ongoing History of New Music
srcs.episode: Catching Up With Twenty One Pilots

podcast.title: Pop-Leaning Rock Sound
podcast.body: Twenty One Pilots are mentioned as an example of an artist whose sound leaned more towards the pop end of rock, a characteristic shared by other successful rock acts in the streaming-dominated 2010s. "But these artists and songs all had one thing in mind. Their sounds leaned more towards the pop end of rock, like 21 Pilots."

srcs.source: The Ongoing History of New Music
srcs.episode: The History of the 2010s Part 1: Rock Struggles Again

podcast.title: Prominent Two-Piece Band
podcast.body: Twenty One Pilots is highlighted as a band that appeared during the rise of two-piece rock acts in the early 2000s, demonstrating the format's growing popularity beyond Canadian groups. "But we also saw the appearance of 21 pilots, the block keys, dressed in dolls, the kills, the Khalifa mods, the Ravianettes, and the load more."

srcs.source: The Ongoing History of New Music
srcs.episode: The 100 Greatest Rock Moments of the Millennium So Far - Part 6: (50-41)

podcast.title: The Banditos (Trench Mythology)
podcast.body: In the fictional world of Dema, the Banditos are portrayed as the heroic figures who seek to liberate the city's inhabitants. They are uniquely identifiable by a specific shade of yellow, a color that the bishops, including Niko, are unable to perceive. "Another within dma is a group called the Banditos. They're the good guys who want to liberate the people of the city."

srcs.source: The Ongoing History of New Music
srcs.episode: Catching Up With Twenty One Pilots

podcast.title: The Skeleton Clique
podcast.body: The band's dedicated fanbase is known as the Skeleton Clique, who pride themselves on being "very, very welcoming" and "the most inclusive clique ever." Members refer to each other as "frens" (spelled F-R-E-N-S) and often use the phrase "Stay Street." "And it helped build the fanbase, which by the way, had become known as the Skeleton clique."

srcs.source: The Ongoing History of New Music
srcs.episode: Catching Up With Twenty One Pilots

podcast.title: USS Precursor Sound
podcast.body: USS's first EP, "From Welding the Sea Drive," released years before, contained sounds and styles that were similar to what Twenty One Pilots would later achieve, implying USS was ahead of the curve. "You can go back to our first EP from welding the C drive and you can hear what 21 pilots is doing in the last couple of years."

srcs.source: The Ongoing History of New Music
srcs.episode: USS In Their Own Words: Part 2

podcast.title: Understanding 21st Century Music Videos
podcast.body: Twenty One Pilots are highlighted as a contemporary artist who "understands the assignment" of music videos in the 21st century. This implies their approach to video production aligns with current trends and demands, leveraging new platforms and creative strategies beyond traditional television channels. "Here's an example of a contemporary artist who understands the assignment of music videos in the 21st century."
